title: Indifference Curves and Consumer Choice
summary: How households choose: preferences and indifference curves, the marginal rate of substitution, the budget line and the consumer optimum – with an interactive demo.

blocks.text: Behind every demand curve are households deciding what to buy. Consumer theory models this choice with two ingredients: **preferences**, described by indifference curves, and the **budget constraint**, given by income and prices. Their combination – the consumer optimum – explains how much of each good a household buys and, in the end, where the demand curve from the previous chapter comes from.

blocks.title: Learning objectives
blocks.text:
- describe preferences with indifference curves and explain their properties
- interpret the marginal rate of substitution (MRS)
- draw the budget line and explain how income and prices move it
- find the consumer optimum graphically and mathematically
- explain how the demand curve follows from the consumer optimum
1. Indifference curves
Consumer theory asks how a household divides its budget between two goods – good 1 with quantity x₁ and good 2 with quantity x₂. Its **preferences** are described with indifference curves.

The set of all bundles of goods (x₁, x₂) that give the household **the same level of utility**. The household is **indifferent** between the bundles on one curve – it does not prefer any of them to another.

blocks.caption: Figure 4: Indifference curves U₁ < U₂ < U₃ – the further from the origin, the higher the utility. The step from A to B illustrates the marginal rate of substitution
blocks.alt: Three convex, downward-sloping indifference curves U1, U2 and U3; an arrow pointing away from the origin shows rising utility. On U2 a step leads from point A to point B: to get more of good 1 (delta x1) the household gives up some of good 2 (delta x2).

blocks.text: Properties

items: **Downward sloping:** If the household gets more of good 1, it must give up some of good 2 to keep its utility constant.
**Further out is better:** Curves further from the origin represent higher utility (non-satiation: more is better).
**They never cross:** An intersection would lie on two utility levels at once – a contradiction to transitive preferences.
**Convex to the origin:** The more of a good the household already has, the less it is willing to give up for another unit of it (diminishing marginal rate of substitution).

blocks.text: 2. The marginal rate of substitution

The amount of good 2 the household would give up for **one additional unit of good 1** while keeping its utility unchanged. Graphically it is the absolute **slope of the indifference curve**; along a convex curve it decreases from the upper left to the lower right.

MRS = −Δx₂ / Δx₁ ≈ −dx₂ / dx₁
    = MU₁ / MU₂

MU: marginal utility
blocks.caption: The MRS equals the ratio of the marginal utilities of the two goods

blocks.title: Special cases
blocks.text:
- **Perfect substitutes** (e.g. two brands of bottled water): the indifference curves are **straight lines**, the MRS is constant.
- **Perfect complements** (e.g. left and right shoes): the indifference curves are **L-shaped** – an extra unit of only one of the two goods adds no utility.
3. The budget line

Which bundle the household actually chooses also depends on its **income m** and the **prices p₁ and p₂**. All bundles it can just afford when spending its entire income lie on the **budget line** (budget constraint).

Budget line:
  p₁·x₁ + p₂·x₂ = m
  ⇔ x₂ = m/p₂ − (p₁/p₂)·x₁

Intercepts: m/p₁ and m/p₂
Slope: −p₁/p₂ (price ratio)
blocks.caption: Higher income shifts the line outwards in parallel; a change in one price rotates it around the other intercept

blocks.text: 4. The consumer optimum

blocks.caption: Figure 5: At the optimum O the budget line touches the highest attainable indifference curve U₂
blocks.alt: Downward-sloping budget line between m/p2 on the vertical and m/p1 on the horizontal axis; the area below it contains the affordable bundles. Indifference curve U2 touches the line at the optimum O at x1* and x2*; U1 crosses the line twice, U3 lies outside the budget.

blocks.text: The household chooses the bundle on the **highest indifference curve it can still reach**. At the optimum O this curve is **tangent** to the budget line, so both have the same slope: the rate at which the household is *willing* to trade (MRS) equals the rate at which it *can* trade in the market (the price ratio). Bundles on U₁ are affordable but not optimal; U₃ lies outside the budget.

Optimum:  MRS = MU₁/MU₂ = p₁/p₂
      ⇔  MU₁/p₁ = MU₂/p₂

(equimarginal principle)
blocks.caption: At the optimum, the last euro spent on each good yields the same additional utility

blocks.title: Worked example: optimum with U = x₁ · x₂
blocks.text:
Given: utility function U = x₁ · x₂, income m = €100, prices p₁ = €2 and p₂ = €5.

1. Marginal utilities: MU₁ = x₂ and MU₂ = x₁ → MRS = x₂ / x₁
2. Optimum condition: x₂ / x₁ = 2 / 5 → x₂ = 0.4 · x₁
3. Substitute into the budget line: 2 · x₁ + 5 · 0.4 · x₁ = 100 → 4 · x₁ = 100 → **x₁ = 25**
4. Hence **x₂ = 10** (check: 2 · 25 + 5 · 10 = 100 ✓) and utility U = 250.
Interactive demo

blocks.title: Try it
blocks.text:
- Double the income **m**: the budget line shifts out in parallel – how do x₁∗ and x₂∗ change?
- Raise the price **p₁**: the budget line rotates inward – x₁∗ falls, while x₂∗ stays the same (a property of this utility function).
- Change **α** to give good 1 more weight: the household spends a larger share of its budget on it.
- Check at every setting: at the optimum the indifference curve just touches the budget line, and MRS = p₁/p₂.

blocks.title: Find the consumer optimum
blocks.caption: Starting point: the worked example above (m = €100, p₁ = €2, p₂ = €5).

blocks.text: *Note:* The demo uses U = x₁^α · x₂^(1−α). With α = 0.5 it describes the same preferences as U = x₁ · x₂ in the worked example – the optimal bundle is identical, only the utility numbers differ. With this utility function the household always spends the share α of its income on good 1.
5. From the consumer optimum to the demand curve

blocks.title: Key point: from the consumer optimum to the demand curve
blocks.text: If you vary the price p₁ and find the new optimum each time, you get the quantity x₁ the household wants at every price – exactly the **individual demand curve** from section 1. Adding up the individual demand curves of all households gives the **market demand curve**.

**Example:** With α = 0.5 and m = 100 the optimal quantity of good 1 is x₁∗ = 0.5 · 100 / p₁ = 50 / p₁. At p₁ = 2 the household buys 25 units, at p₁ = 4 only 12.5 – the higher the price, the lower the quantity: a downward-sloping demand curve. Check it in the demo by moving p₁.
Key terms

rows: how a household ranks bundles of goods
extra utility from one more unit of a good
slope of the indifference curve, MU₁/MU₂
bundles that cost exactly the income m
tangency of budget line and indifference curve
MU per euro is equal across goods at the optimum

blocks.text: Self-test

blocks.front: Why can indifference curves never cross?
blocks.back: An intersection would lie on two different utility levels at the same time – this contradicts transitive preferences (and the principle that more is better).

blocks.front: What is the marginal rate of substitution (MRS)?
blocks.back: The amount of good 2 the household would give up for one additional unit of good 1 without losing utility – the absolute slope of the indifference curve (= MU₁ / MU₂).

blocks.front: Which condition holds at the consumer optimum?
blocks.back: The indifference curve is tangent to the budget line: **MRS = p₁ / p₂** (equivalently: MU₁ / p₁ = MU₂ / p₂).

blocks.front: How does the budget line react when the price of good 1 rises?
blocks.back: It rotates inward around its intercept on the x₂ axis (m/p₂) and becomes steeper – its slope is −p₁/p₂.

blocks.question: Which properties do well-behaved indifference curves have?

options.text: Curves further from the origin represent lower utility.
They are convex to the origin.

blocks.explanation: Curves further from the origin contain more of both goods – so they represent **higher** utility.

blocks.question: At the consumer optimum …

options.text: the budget is not fully spent.

blocks.explanation: At the optimum the highest attainable indifference curve is tangent to the budget line, so their slopes – the MRS and the price ratio – are equal. Since more is better, the whole budget is spent.

blocks.question: U = x₁^0.5 · x₂^0.5, income m = 120, prices p₁ = 3 and p₂ = 4. How much of good 1 does the household buy?
blocks.explanation: With this utility function the household spends half of its income on each good: x₁∗ = 0.5 · 120 / 3 = 20 (and x₂∗ = 0.5 · 120 / 4 = 15). Check it in the demo.
